{{Short description|Analytic function in mathematics}}
[[File:Lacunary domain coloring.png|thumb|Domain coloring of the 128th partial sum of the lacunary function <math>\sum_{n=0}^\infty z^{2^n}</math>.]]
In [[complex analysis|analysis]], a '''lacunary function''' or '''series''' is an [[analytic function]] containing many zero coefficients in its [[Basis (linear algebra)|basis]] decomposition. A series can be lacunary in the sense of having Hadamard or Fabry gaps (or lacunae). They are associated with the [[Hadamard gap theorem]] and the [[Fabry gap theorem]] stating that a lacunary [[power series|Taylor series]] cannot be [[analytic continuation|analytically continued]] outside its [[radius of convergence|disk of convergence]]. More recent investigations examine lacunary [[Fourier series]] as well.

The word ''lacunary'' is derived from [[wiktionary:lacuna|lacuna]] (''pl.'' lacunae), meaning gap, or vacancy.

== A simple example ==

Pick an integer <math>a \geq 2</math>. Consider the following function defined by a power series:

:<math>
f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty z^{a^n} = z + z^a + z^{a^2} + z^{a^3} + z^{a^4} + \cdots\,
</math>

The power series converges locally uniform on any open domain |''z''| < 1. This can be proved by comparing ''f'' with the [[geometric series]], which is absolutely convergent when |''z''| < 1. So ''f'' is analytic on the open [[unit disk]]. Nevertheless, ''f'' has [[Dense set|dense]] singularities on the [[unit circle]], and cannot be analytically continued outside of the open unit disk, as the following argument demonstrates.

Clearly ''f'' has a singularity at ''z'' = 1, because

:<math>
f(1) = 1 + 1 + 1 + \cdots\,
</math>

is a [[divergent series]]. But if ''z'' is allowed to be non-real, problems arise, since

:<math>
f(z^a) = f(z) - z \qquad f\bigl(z^{a^2}\bigr) = f(z^a) - z^a \qquad f\bigl(z^{a^3}\bigr) = f\bigl(z^{a^2}\bigr) - z^{a^2} \qquad \cdots \qquad f\bigl(z^{a^{n+1}}\bigr) = f\bigl(z^{a^n}\bigr)-z^{a^n}
</math>

we can see that ''f'' has a singularity at a point ''z'' when ''z''<sup>a</sup> = 1, and also when ''z''<sup>a<sup>2</sup></sup> = 1. By the induction suggested by the above equations, ''f'' must have a singularity at each of the ''a''<sup>''n''</sup>-th [[root of unity|roots of unity]] for all natural numbers ''n.'' The set of all such singularities is [[dense set|dense]] on the unit circle; so it is impossible to define ''f'' on any [[open set]] containing the unit circle, making analytic continuation impossible as well.<ref>(Whittaker and Watson, 1927, p. 98) This example apparently originated with Weierstrass.</ref>

== An elementary result ==
The argument above shows that certain series define lacunary functions. What is not so evident is that the gaps between the powers of ''z'' can grow much more slowly, and the resulting series will still define a lacunary function. To make this notion more precise some additional notation is needed.

We write

:<math>
f(z) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_kz^{\lambda_k} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n z^n\,
</math>

where ''b''<sub>''n''</sub> = ''a''<sub>''k''</sub> when ''n'' = &lambda;<sub>''k''</sub>, and ''b''<sub>''n''</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 otherwise. The stretches where the coefficients ''b''<sub>''n''</sub> in the second series are all zero are the ''lacunae'' in the coefficients. The monotonically increasing sequence of positive natural numbers {&lambda;<sub>''k''</sub>} specifies the powers of ''z'' which are in the power series for ''f''(''z'').

Now a theorem of [[Jaques Hadamard|Hadamard]] can be stated.<ref>(Mandelbrojt and Miles, 1927)</ref> If

:<math>
\frac{\lambda_k}{\lambda_{k-1}} > 1 + \delta \,
</math>

for all ''k'', where ''&delta;'' > 0 is an arbitrary positive constant, then ''f''(''z'') is a lacunary function that cannot be [[Analytic continuation|continued]] outside its circle of convergence. In other words, the sequence {&lambda;<sub>''k''</sub>} doesn't have to grow as fast as 2<sup>''k''</sup> for ''f''(''z'') to be a lacunary function &ndash; it just has to grow as fast as some [[geometric progression]] (1&nbsp;+&nbsp;&delta;)<sup>''k''</sup>. A series for which &lambda;<sub>''k''</sub> grows this quickly is said to contain '''Hadamard gaps'''; see the [[Hadamard gap theorem]] and its generalization, the [[Fabry gap theorem]].

== Lacunary trigonometric series ==

Mathematicians have also investigated the properties of lacunary trigonometric series

:<math>
S((\lambda_k)_k,\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k \cos(\lambda_k\theta) \qquad 
S((\lambda_k)_k,\theta,\omega) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k \cos(\lambda_k\theta + \omega) \,
</math>

for which the &lambda;<sub>''k''</sub> are far apart. Here the coefficients ''a''<sub>''k''</sub> are real numbers. In this context, attention has been focused on criteria sufficient to guarantee convergence of the trigonometric series [[almost everywhere]] (that is, for almost every value of the angle ''&theta;'' and of the distortion factor ''&omega;'').
*[[Andrey Kolmogorov|Kolmogorov]] showed that if the sequence {''&lambda;''<sub>''k''</sub>} contains Hadamard gaps, then the series ''S''(''&lambda;''<sub>''k''</sub>,&nbsp;''&theta;'',&nbsp;''&omega;'') converges almost everywhere if and only if <math>
\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k^2
</math> converges.

*[[Antoni Zygmund|Zygmund]] showed under the same condition that ''S''(''&lambda;''<sub>''k''</sub>,&nbsp;''&theta;'',&nbsp;''&omega;'') is not a Fourier series representing an [[integrable function]] when this sum of squares of the ''a''<sub>''k''</sub> is a divergent series.<ref>(Fukuyama and Takahashi, 1999)</ref>
